doc.title: Bob Rosengarden interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 6, 1996

title: Benny Goodman: a mean but great player, and the Japan tour
summary: He describes Goodman's cruelty, firing and the 'Am I mad at you?' call, plus Goodman imitators on a Japan tour.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Didn’t you do a thing with Benny Goodman when Igor Stravinsky was around too? What was that like?

It was quite an experience. I think about it every once in a while. Benny was a difficult man to deal with, to work for. He was Jewish but he was Adolph Hitler. He was mean, and different and callous and mean, and played his buns off. He was an inspiration when he played. But he didn’t like people. He didn’t care. There was a gesture that all of us knew meant go away. Not a nice man. Played better than anybody. And they won’t let his memory die. I just did a tour of Japan, a two week tour just recently a few months ago, my wife and I had a great time. Peanuts Hucko was Benny, he became Benny, because Benny had died, and there were lots of Bennies around. Abe Most from California, he does a Benny imitation too; Walt Levinsky does it; a couple of other clarinet players too. Sol Yaged tried too but he wasn’t that good a clarinet player.
Well you have to be fairly accomplished.

Oh, yeah, Benny was a wonderful player. Of course he fired me. He fired me many times, I mean he fired everybody. One story I remember he called me, and he had a strange voice on the phone, “Bobby” I mean his voice, “Bobby, this is Benny.” And I said, “Yes, I know.” He said, “Bobby, tell me something?” True story. And I said, “What is it, Benny?” He says, “Am I mad at you?” And I said, “I beg your pardon?” And he said, “Am I mad at you? I seem to remember that I’m mad at you.” I said, “I don’t think so, Benny, the last time we worked together was a long time ago, but I don’t remember throwing a cymbal at you or you throwing your clarinet at me.” He says, “Well, never © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-
mind, can you do—” such-and-such. And then he never called me again. I mean then I did the job, whatever it was, and he just [inaudible]. But, “Bobby, am I mad at you?”
That’s funny because you know what that voice reminds me of? It reminds me of the woman who played Benny’s mother in the movie they made about him.
But the woman who played his mother talked just like that.
Well somebody was being funny because somebody talked like, “Bobby,” you know and he had these gestures, these strange gestures. He was odd. But he played good, God he played good.
Well he has a whole chapter devoted to him in the Jazz Anecdotes.

Oh there are stories that are so popular now. Everybody, I mean every once in a while we go the jazz festivals all over the country which are quite popular, all over the world. On this tour of Japan there were a lot of alumnus of Benny’s bands of one time or another, and of course you get a couple of drinks of saki and you sit around and tell Benny Goodman stories, and fall on the floor. It was fun.
